top_story: Trump’s March threat to destroy Iran’s power grid if Tehran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz set the frame for Iran’s vow of wider regional retaliation, and that escalatory logic is now playing out in the Gulf. By 7–9 May, a month-old ceasefire had narrowed into a brittle pause as US and Iranian forces exchanged strikes in and around Hormuz, showing that de-escalation mechanisms are failing even when both sides signal interest in containing the fight. The standoff is structurally hard to sustain: Iran absorbs acute economic pressure from disrupted shipping and energy flows, while Washington faces mounting costs from a confrontation tied to its own coercive strategy. The clearest takeaway is that Hormuz has become less a stable ceasefire line than a recurring trigger point where limited clashes can quickly spill into a broader regional crisis with immediate civilian and market consequences.
